An ASSUMPTION gives its basis.\n32\t\n33\t**Missing inputs:** the unknowns that would change the plan most, and any assumption the phase\n34\torder rests on.\n35\t\n36\t## 2. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_014nKxft8vN9zur6orhMbuHc","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\nsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n\n## 1. Dependency kinds\n\n| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n\nCommon misses:\n\n- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n\n## 2. Validation gates\n\nFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n\n| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n\nShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\nso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n\nA good acceptance threshold:\n\n- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n  security, or legal judgment;\n- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n\nAnti-patterns:\n\n- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n  correct, or affordable enough.\n- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n  UNKNOWN has no number.\n- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n  sublayer.\n- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n\n## 3. Reversibility\n\n| Tier | Examples |\n|---|---|\n| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n\nCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\nbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\nundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\nirreversible operation.\n\nBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\nprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n\nSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\ninterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\nraw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\nthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\non every row from day one.\n\n## 4. Budgets\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n\nRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\nis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n\n## 5. Methodology exceptions\n\n| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n\nNot exceptions:\n\n- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n- Brownfield work. The order below is deliberate:\n4\tdefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\n5\tis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\n6\ttreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\n7\tright after it, before any external exposure.\n8\t\n9\tAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\n10\thypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\n11\tconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\n12\trarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\n13\tA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n14\t\n15\t## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n16\t\n17\t### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\n18\tUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\n19\tall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\n20\timpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n21\t- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n22\t- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n23\t- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n24\t- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n25\t- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n26\t  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n27\t  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n28\t  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n29\t  design, not by filtering.\n30\t\n31\t### 2. Cost + latency budget\n32\tAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n33\t- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n34\t- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n35\t- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n36\t  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n37\t  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n38\t- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n39\t\n40\t### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\n41\tDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\n42\tirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\n43\tchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n44\t- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n45\t  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n46\t\n47\t## Capability order (build after defenses)\n48\t\n49\t### 4. Retrieval\n50\tGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\n51\tembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\n52\tpermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n53\t- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n54\t  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n55\t\n56\t### 5. Model access\n57\tA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\n58\tstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n59\t- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n60\t  at the stated threshold.\n61\t\n62\t### 6. Memory\n63\tWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\n64\tan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n65\t- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n66\t\n67\t### 7. Orchestration\n68\tHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n69\t- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n70\t  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n71\t\n72\t### 8. Routing\n73\tSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n74\t- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n75\t  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n76\t\n77\t### 9. Feedback\n78\tCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\n79\tretrieval tuning, or training data.\n80\t- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n81\t  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n82\t  poisoning path.)\n83\t\n84\t## Notes\n85\t- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n86\t  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n87\t  and eval scores — from day zero.\n88\t- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n89\t  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). The order below is deliberate:\ndefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\nis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\ntreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\nright after it, before any external exposure.\n\nAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\nhypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\nconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\nrarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\nA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n\n## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n\n### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\nUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\nall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\nimpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n  design, not by filtering.\n\n### 2. Cost + latency budget\nAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n\n### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\nDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\nirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\nchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n\n## Capability order (build after defenses)\n\n### 4. Retrieval\nGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\nembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\npermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n\n### 5. Model access\nA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\nstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n  at the stated threshold.\n\n### 6. Memory\nWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\nan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n\n### 7. Orchestration\nHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n\n### 8. Routing\nSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n\n### 9. Feedback\nCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\nretrieval tuning, or training data.\n- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n  poisoning path.)\n\n## Notes\n- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n  and eval scores — from day zero.\n- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). Fine-tuning a model is usually R2;\n  training on customer or personal data is R3.\n","numLines":91,"startLine":1,"totalLines":91}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_5gmvxoyeg7c7apeuwa4yywycczlexvjoy2doodz6nj42ompux2tq","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Real-time card-transaction fraud detection\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n\nThe request leaves out three inputs that would change the order of phases. Rather than stop, I assumed the following. Each line says what changes if the assumption is wrong.\n- **A1, our role.** We are a card issuer (or issuer-processor) deciding authorizations. If we are an acquirer or merchant instead, the decision point moves to the gateway or checkout, and PCI scope and label sources change.\n- **A2, inline decisions.** \"Real-time\" means the score affects the approve/decline decision during authorization. If you only want alerts after authorization, V4 and V5 become exit checks and Phase 2 gets much smaller.\n- **A3, brownfield.** An authorization host and an existing fraud system (\"incumbent\": rules engine or vendor score) already run in production. If not, there is no fallback decision, so V4 must fall back to a static rules floor and V7 has no baseline to beat.\n\n- **What:** a streaming pipeline that scores each card authorization within the authorization deadline. It returns approve, step-up or decline with reason codes, and learns from fraud labels (chargebacks, cardholder fraud reports, analyst outcomes).\n- **Type:** software, streaming data infrastructure, and a predictive ML model (not generative or agentic). Brownfield. Not a small build: it handles real money and regulated data (PCI DSS, personal data).\n- **Dominant constraint:** latency under a hard authorization deadline. Decision correctness is a close second, and PCI DSS shapes the trust boundaries.\n- **Worst failure:** the new path wrongly declines legitimate transactions at scale, through a bad model, a bad rule push, or failing closed on timeout. Cardholders get stranded at tills, and that harm cannot be undone. Guarded by V4. The second worst is the card number (PAN) leaking into pipeline stores, guarded by V2.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Scoring latency (at auth host, including feature fetch) | p99 ≤ 50 ms; hard timeout 80 ms, then incumbent decides | ASSUMPTION: leaves most of the auth host's budget free; confirm with auth platform owner | V0 records the floor; V5 |\n| Network response deadline | — | UNKNOWN: the scheme's stand-in timeout for our BINs (bank ID ranges); auth platform owner; needed in Phase 2 | V4 |\n| Throughput | 3× measured peak-hour authorizations per second | BASELINE peak from auth host logs (Phase 0) × ASSUMPTION multiplier for seasonal peak plus growth | V5 |\n| Authorization availability | No drop below the auth host's current availability | BASELINE (Phase 0) | V3, V4 |\n| Scoring coverage | ≥ 99.9% of authorizations scored within timeout | ASSUMPTION: an unscored transaction falls back to the incumbent, so a miss costs only the incumbent's quality; confirm with Head of Fraud | Phase 2 SLO, V5 |\n| Detection quality | Fraud value caught ≥ incumbent + uplift, at false-positive ratio ≤ incumbent | Incumbent: BASELINE (backtest). Uplift: UNKNOWN, Head of Fraud supplies it before Phase 4 | V7 |\n| Incremental declines from new path | ≤ 0.5 pp above the segment's baseline decline rate | ASSUMPTION: about the incumbent's normal day-to-day variation; confirm with Head of Fraud | V4, Phase 5 cohort checks |\n| RPO / RTO | Decision log RPO 0; feature state RTO ≤ 1 h (rebuilt from the event log; incumbent decides meanwhile) | ASSUMPTION: decisions are dispute and audit evidence; confirm with Compliance | Phase 1, Phase 3 drill |\n| Retention | Event and decision log ≥ 13 months for training; regulatory maximum or minimum unknown | 13 months: ASSUMPTION (one seasonal cycle plus label maturity). Regulatory: UNKNOWN, Compliance supplies it in Phase 1 | Phase 1 |\n| Operational complexity | ≤ 4 new runtime components (event log, stream processor, state store, scoring service); 24/7 on-call shared with the auth platform | ASSUMPTION | Phase 2 exit |\n\n**Missing inputs:**\n- A1, A2 and A3 above.\n- 12–18 months of history joinable to fraud labels (tested by V1).\n- The scheme timeout value.\n- Jurisdiction: data residency, the model-risk regime (e.g. SR 11-7 or the EU equivalent), GDPR Art. 22 on automated decisions, and PSD2 transaction-risk-analysis exemptions if in the EU.\n- ML and streaming staffing (needed for the build-vs-buy row).\n- The Head of Fraud's uplift target and risk appetite.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Phase 0 auth-host hook | Change-board approval for the auth host; a production account in the cardholder-data environment; allow-listed staff test cards (ASSUMED) | organizational | deployed |\n| V1 label-join analysis | Approval to access historical auth and dispute data in the warehouse (start in Phase 0) | organizational | built |\n| Event schema v1 freeze (Phase 1) | V1: the network transaction ID that disputes reference must be in the schema | structural (surprising) + validation | specified |\n| Mirroring all cardholders' traffic | V2: PAN boundary, plus QSA/ISA review and the DPIA (data-protection impact assessment) | risk-security + organizational | exposed |\n| Widening the tap beyond one node | V3 | risk-security | deployed |\n| Inline calls at scale; any enforcement | V4 fail-safe, V5 latency | risk-security + validation | exposed |\n| V4 threshold | Scheme timeout value (auth platform owner) | organizational | specified |\n| Model training on backfilled features | V6 parity | validation | specified |\n| V7 threshold | Uplift target (Head of Fraud) | organizational | specified |\n| Enforcement (Phase 5) | V7 uplift (also the economic case), V8 model-risk sign-off (ASSUMED applicable) | validation + economic + organizational | exposed |\n| Step-up / referral | Existing case-management and cardholder-alerting APIs and their capacity (ASSUMED) | runtime | deployed |\n| Build-vs-buy commitment | V1, V7 | decision | committed |\n\nEvery kind has at least one instance. All brownfield dependencies are ASSUMED until the Phase 1 discovery task confirms them.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Sync vs async (decision placement) | R2: flag-reversible, but auth-host integration and latency work take weeks | Async mirror feeds the features. A sync inline score call with a hard timeout runs in shadow until V4/V5 pass, and enforces only from Phase 5 | Scoring fits inside the auth budget | V5, V4 | V5 fails, then post-auth alert plus block-next-transaction for the affected segments |\n| Failure mode | R3 by harm: minutes of failing closed means mass declines | Fail to the incumbent's decision. Never decline because the new path failed | The incumbent stays running (A3) | V4 | Only if the incumbent is retired: fall back to a static rules floor inside the auth host, re-gated |\n| Consistency vs availability of entity state | R2: state-store redesign | Availability: score on last-known state. Per-card counters have a single writer per token partition. Merchant and device aggregates are eventual, with staleness p99 ≤ 1 s (ASSUMPTION) | Card-testing bursts are visible within 1 s | V6 staleness clause, plus a burst-replay check in Phase 3 | Bursts missed, or staleness above 1 s at load, then synchronous merchant counters |\n| Monolith vs services | R2 | One scoring service doing feature fetch, rules, model and policy in-process. One stream job. Offline training kept separate | In-process composition is needed for latency; one team | V5 | Fraud ops need an independent rule cadence, then hot-loaded rule config (still not a separate service) |\n| Build vs buy | R2 for build (the seams carry over to a vendor); buying is R3 (multi-year contract, data held at the vendor) | Build on open components. Incumbent and network scores (e.g. Visa/Mastercard risk scores) become features and the fallback | Enough labels; in-house ML and streaming staff | V1, then V7 | V1 fails, V7 fails twice, or no staff: buy a vendor behind the same hook and schema |\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: a PAN in a log or store cannot be un-leaked | PAN and sensitive authentication data never leave the auth host. The pipeline sees only card token, BIN and derived values; no names; data minimized; DPIA done | The existing token vault covers every authorization | V2 | V2 finds a PAN: stop the mirror, purge, fix the edge. A feature needs the PAN: compute it in the auth host and pass only the derived value |\n| Event schema and identifiers | R3: labels, training data and the decision log build up on it from Phase 1 | Versioned Protobuf in a schema registry, expand/contract changes only. Keys: card token, network transaction ID, auth message ID | Dispute records carry the network transaction ID | V1 | V1 join rate below threshold: add the missing key or fix dispute capture before the freeze |\n| Training/serving feature parity | R2 | Features defined once in Flink; backfill replays history through the same job | History can be replayed into schema v1 | V6 | V6 fails, then train only on features logged at serving time |\n| Coexistence and cutover | R2: per-segment flag | The auth host stays system of record for decisions. Shadow first, then canary by card-token-hash cohort. A permanent 2% control holdout stays on the incumbent. The incumbent is not retired (§10) | The incumbent keeps running | V4, V7, Phase 5 cohort checks | A cohort check trips: revert that cohort |\n\n**R1 defaults:**\n- Model family: gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM), served via ONNX Runtime.\n- Online store: Aerospike or Redis behind an interface (rebuildable from the log).\n- Event log: Kafka with replication factor 3 across availability zones.\n- Retraining: monthly.\n- Tooling: MLflow registry, OpenTelemetry, Prometheus/Grafana, Argo CD, Terraform.\n\n**N/A:**\n- Prompt+RAG vs fine-tune, and hosted vs self-hosted LLM: there is no LLM.\n- Tenancy: single issuer (ASSUMPTION).\n- Rehost/replatform/refactor: the incumbent is not migrated; the new capability runs alongside it.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n\n- **Real request:** a small real purchase on an allow-listed staff test card. The scheme authorization request reaches the auth host. The auth host sends the incumbent's normal response to the network. It also gets the new path's shadow decision (score, reason code, model `stub-0`) and writes it to its audit record.\n- **Tiers:**\n  - auth-host hook (sync call, 80 ms timeout, token-only payload)\n  - scoring service (stub rule over one feature: card transaction count in 24 h)\n  - online state store, updated by a Flink job reading the Kafka event topic (fed by the auth-host tap)\n  - decision-log topic sunk to the warehouse\n  - one test case in the existing case-management tool\n  - one test fraud report on the same transaction from the dispute system, joined by network transaction ID (ASSUMED test mode; otherwise moves to Phase 3)\n- **Deploy, log, monitor, roll back:**\n  - Terraform and Argo CD deploy signed images. The auth-host hook ships through its own change-board release, flag off by default.\n  - One OpenTelemetry trace keyed to the auth message ID. Logs carry tokens only and are classified as cardholder-data-environment data.\n  - Alerts fire on scoring timeouts.\n  - Rollback is an Argo CD revert plus the auth-host flag.\n- **Who can reach it:** only allow-listed test-card tokens. The incumbent decides every transaction.\n\nExit check (V0): see §6.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n**Phase 1: Event substrate and data boundary (shadow, async only)**\n- **Unlocks:** real tokenized traffic for features, replay and load tests.\n- **Depends on:** V0, V1.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Discover dependents: the incumbent, case management, the dispute system, cardholder alerting, warehouse feeds. Mark each CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n  2. Freeze event schema v1 and the decision-log schema (score, reason codes, model and rule versions, feature-vector hash, latency, fallback flag).\n  3. Put PAN-boundary controls and continuous data-loss-prevention (DLP) scanning in place and complete the DPIA, then run V2 on the staff cohort.\n  4. Run the tap on one auth-host node (V3), then all nodes. Widen mirrored traffic from staff cards to one BIN range to all.\n  5. Set retention TTLs once Compliance supplies the figure.\n  6. Build replay tooling and record a tokenized traffic corpus.\n- **System of record:** the auth host. Sync runs one way, auth host to event log.\n- **Rollback:** tap flag per node; purge topics. Nothing affects decisions.\n- **Exit check:** V2 and V3 pass; consumer lag < 1 s at peak.\n\n**Phase 2: Decision-safety defenses and budgets**\n- **Unlocks:** inline calls at scale and, later, enforcement.\n- **Depends on:** Phase 1, V2, V3.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Get the scheme timeout value.\n  2. Build fallback in the auth host: hard timeout, incumbent decision on any error, kill switch per segment.\n  3. Build a policy layer:\n     - restricted action set\n     - decline caps\n     - a circuit breaker comparing the new decision rate with the incumbent's, per segment\n  4. Add ingress validation, an adversarial test suite (card testing, threshold probing, malformed fields) and generic response codes, so the score can't be reverse-engineered from responses.\n  5. Enforce four-eyes approval in the pipeline for rule, threshold and model changes.\n  6. Build a load harness on the replay corpus (V5).\n  7. Run fault injection and a production game day on the staff cohort (V4).\n- **Rollback:** everything is behind flags.\n- **Exit check:** V4 and V5 pass.\n\n**Phase 3: Features, entity state, labels**\n- **Unlocks:** model training.\n- **Depends on:** Phase 2, V1, V5 (the feature budget).\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Get the uplift target from the Head of Fraud.\n  2. Build features in Flink:\n     - velocity per card, account, merchant, device, MCC and country\n     - deviation from the card's normal spend\n     - merchant risk\n     - incumbent and network scores\n  3. Build the online state store keyed by token.\n  4. Backfill by replaying history through the same job.\n  5. Enforce in this order: staff cohort, then 1% of tokens in one segment, then 5%, 25%, 100%.\n     - Pick the first segment where the step-up flow exists (e.g. card-not-present).\n     - Each step runs ≥ 7 days including a weekend peak.\n     - Each step must pass the cohort checks: incremental declines within cap, false-positive ratio ≤ BASELINE, complaints ≤ control, latency within budget.\n- **Rollback:** per-cohort flag back to the incumbent, plus the automatic breaker. No point of no return, because the incumbent is kept.\n- **Exit check:** all traffic except the holdout is enforced, with every step's checks passed.\n\n**Phase 6: Feedback and retraining**\n- **Unlocks:** sustained model quality.\n- **Depends on:** Phase 5 with ≥ 60 days of matured labels.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Review labels before training (friendly fraud, analyst error).\n  2. Retrain monthly from reproducible snapshots.\n  3. Evaluate each challenger with the V7 method, using the holdout to correct selection bias.\n  4. Promote with four-eyes approval plus the model-risk change process.\n  5. Add drift alerts (population stability index, PSI).\n- **Rollback:** the previous champion stays in the registry.\n- **Exit check:** one full cycle (retrain, evaluate, promote or reject) completes with lineage recorded.\n\n## 6. Deliberately deferred\n\n- **Retiring the incumbent (point of no return).** Pull forward when the new path has run at 100% for ≥ 2 quarters with V7 thresholds holding, or when the vendor contract comes up for renewal. It then needs its own gate: rehearse the static-rules-floor fallback, a go/no-go threshold, approval from the Head of Fraud and CRO, and contract termination named as the point of no return.\n- **Segment models and routing (card-present, card-not-present, ATM).** Pull forward when one segment trails the others on V7 metrics by an agreed margin.\n- **Graph / fraud-ring features.** Pull forward when ring-driven losses make up a material share of fraud.\n- **Deep sequence models.** Pull forward when the GBDT plateaus across two retrain cycles.\n- **Multi-region active-active.** Pull forward when the business commits to an availability target that single-region multi-AZ cannot meet.\n- **3DS/ACS (online card-authentication) step-up integration.** Pull forward if we run the ACS and card-not-present fraud dominates.\n- **LLM analyst assistant.** Pull forward when analyst queue load becomes the bottleneck.
